{{Short description|Graph made from a subset of another graph's nodes and their edges}}

In [[graph theory]], an '''induced subgraph''' of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] is another graph, formed from a [[subset]] of the [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] of the graph and ''all'' of the edges, from the original graph, connecting pairs of vertices in that subset.

==Definition==
Formally, let <math>G=(V,E) </math> be any graph, and let <math>S\subseteq V </math> be any subset of vertices of {{mvar|G}}. Then the induced subgraph <math>G[S] </math> is the graph whose vertex set is <math>S </math> and whose edge set consists of all of the edges in <math>E </math> that have both endpoints in <math>S </math>.<ref>{{citation|title=Graph Theory|volume=173|series=Graduate texts in mathematics|first=Reinhard|last=Diestel|publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=2006|isbn=9783540261834|pages=3–4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aR2TMYQr2CMC&pg=PA3}}.</ref> That is, for any two vertices <math>u,v\in S </math>, <math>u </math> and <math>v </math> are adjacent in <math>G[S] </math> if and only if they are adjacent in <math>G </math>. The same definition works for [[undirected graph]]s, [[directed graph]]s, and even [[multigraph]]s.

The induced subgraph <math>G[S] </math> may also be called the subgraph induced in <math>G </math> by <math>S </math>, or (if context makes the choice of <math>G </math> unambiguous) the induced subgraph of <math>S </math>.

==Examples==
Important types of induced subgraphs include the following.
[[File:Snake in the box.svg|thumb|The [[snake-in-the-box]] problem concerns the longest [[induced path]]s in [[hypercube graph]]s]]
*[[Induced path]]s are induced subgraphs that are [[path (graph theory)|paths]]. The [[shortest path]] between any two vertices in an unweighted graph is always an induced path, because any additional edges between pairs of vertices that could cause it to be not induced would also cause it to be not shortest. Conversely, in [[distance-hereditary graph]]s, every induced path is a shortest path.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Howorka | first = Edward
 | title = A characterization of distance-hereditary graphs
 | journal = The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics |series=Second Series
 | volume = 28 | issue = 112 | year = 1977 | pages = 417–420
 | mr = 0485544
 | doi = 10.1093/qmath/28.4.417}}.</ref>
*[[Induced cycle]]s are induced subgraphs that are [[cycle (graph theory)|cycles]]. The [[girth (graph theory)|girth]] of a graph is defined by the length of its shortest cycle, which is always an induced cycle. According to the [[strong perfect graph theorem]], induced cycles and their [[complement graph|complements]] play a critical role in the characterization of [[perfect graph]]s.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Chudnovsky | first1 = Maria | author1-link = Maria Chudnovsky
 | last2 = Robertson | first2 = Neil | author2-link = Neil Robertson (mathematician)
 | last3 = Seymour | first3 = Paul | author3-link = Paul Seymour (mathematician)
 | last4 = Thomas | first4 = Robin | author4-link = Robin Thomas (mathematician)
 | doi = 10.4007/annals.2006.164.51
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Annals of Mathematics]]
 | pages = 51–229
 | title = The strong perfect graph theorem
 | volume = 164
 | year = 2006
 | mr = 2233847| arxiv = math/0212070}}.</ref>
*[[clique (graph theory)|Cliques]] and [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent sets]] are induced subgraphs that are respectively [[complete graph]]s or [[edgeless graph]]s.
*[[Induced matching]]s are induced subgraphs that are [[Matching (graph theory)|matchings]].
*The [[Neighbourhood (graph theory)|neighborhood]] of a vertex is the induced subgraph of all vertices adjacent to it.

==Computation==
The [[induced subgraph isomorphism problem]] is a form of the [[subgraph isomorphism problem]] in which the goal is to test whether one graph can be found as an induced subgraph of another. Because it includes the [[clique problem]] as a special case, it is [[NP-complete]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Johnson | first = David S.
 | doi = 10.1016/0196-6774(85)90012-4
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Journal of Algorithms
 | mr = 800733
 | pages = 434–451
 | title = The NP-completeness column: an ongoing guide
 | volume = 6
 | year = 1985}}.</ref>
